title: Language Comprehension
before:
Much of the Language Comprehension section is similar to Scarborough's Rope. Newer categories, found in the Active View of Reading based on reading science, are Cultural and Other Content Knowledge and Theory of Mind. Cultural and Other Content Knowledge includes work on the role of students' prior and background knowledge to improve reading. Theory of Mind refers to a reader's ability to empathize with characters or people in books. 
Each accordion below has self-paced asynchronous professional learning modules with a mix of video and text resources, opportunities for application and reflection, and contact hours.
 If you would like a contact hour for your work, please e-mail Kathy.Bertini@maine.gov

 

Cultural and Other Content Knowledge

Use the links below to access the asynchronous professional learning modules and explore the resources.

  • Culturally Responsive Teaching & The Brain by Zaretta Hammond
  • Concept Foundations and Formation module focuses on how to make connections within and across content areas, supporting student learning, engagement, and transfer of knowledge and skills.
  • Overarching Ideas module focuses on how to identify the big ideas to make connections within and across content areas.
  • Teaching for Transfer webpage provides 2 pathways for supporting instruction to engage learners in connecting and transferring their learning.
    • Path 1: Learning That Transfers - Acquire, Connect, Transfer module based on the work of Julie Stern
    • Path 2: Make Learning Visible - Surface, Deep, Transfer module based on the work of John Hattie
Reading-specific Background Knowledge

Use the links below to access the asynchronous professional learning modules and explore the resources.

  • AIM Steps to Literacy Learning Modules - Module 5: Language Comprehension & Written Expression
  • AIM Steps to Literacy Learning Modules - Module 8: Specialized Reading Knowledge Bundle - English Learners
  • Improving Adolescent Literacy: Effective Classroom and Intervention Practices (WWC Practice Guide) provides four evidence-based recommendations that teachers can use to deliver reading interventions to meet the diverse needs of their students.
  • Adolescent Literacy Intervention Selection Tool (A-List Tool) provides information about literacy programs for grades 4-12 to help educators make informed intervention program choices.
Verbal Reasoning

Use the links below to access the asynchronous professional learning modules and explore the resources.

  • Shifting the Balance: 6 Ways to Bring the Science of Reading into the Balanced Literacy Classroom (K-2), by Jan Burkins and Kari Yates - "Shifting the Balance" is a literacy book that provides practical strategies for teachers to bridge the gap between traditional phonics-based instruction and balanced literacy approaches. It aims to improve student outcomes by integrating research-based practices and offering actionable steps for enhancing reading instruction.
    • Shifting the Balance: Grade K-2 Downloads webpage: Dialogic Conversation to Develop Oral Language
  • Shifting the Balance, Grades 3-5: 6 Ways to Bring the Science of Reading into the Balanced Literacy Classroom, by Katie Cunningham, Jan Burkins, and Kari Yates - "Shifting the Balance" is a literacy book that provides practical strategies for teachers to bridge the gap between traditional phonics-based instruction and balanced literacy approaches. It aims to improve student outcomes by integrating research-based practices and offering actionable steps for enhancing reading instruction.
  • Florida Center for Reading Research - provides resources on metaphors and idioms
Language Structure

Use the links below to access the asynchronous professional learning modules and explore the resources.

  • Executive Skills and Reading Comprehension by Kelly Cartwright.  
  • Why Do I Have to Read this? by Cris Tovani 
Theory of Mind

Use the links below to access the asynchronous professional learning modules and explore the resources.

  • The Science of Reading Progresses: Communicating Advances Beyond the Simple View of Reading - provides a definition and explanation of the Theory of Mind.

  • Executive Skills and Reading Comprehension by Kelly Cartwright.  In Ch 7, Cartwright discusses the role of Theory of Mind on comprehension.
  • Why Do I Have to Read this? by Cris Tovani 
  • Reading Rockets - article on Exploring the Theory of Mind, Weak Central Cohesion, and Executive Functioning in ASD
  • Reading Rockets - Picture Book and Emotional Literacy

notes: 1 section header — too few for a contents list.
651 words with no section headers at all — the biggest single improvement available here.

decisions.label: Set an over-long heading as the paragraph it is
decisions.why: 2 headings run past 100 characters — the longest here is 437. "Much of the Language Comprehension section is similar to…" is body text that was set as a heading to make it stand out, so it is announced as a section of the page and, at h2, written into the contents list as a link. It becomes a paragraph. Any anchor on it is kept, so existing links still land, and not a word changes.

decisions.label: Rebuild the heading outline
decisions.why: 1 heading sits at a level the page never opens — "If you would like a contact hour for your work, " is an h6 with no h5 above it, so it is neither announced nor styled as the sub-section it is. Each heading moves to one level below whatever encloses it.

decisions.label: Turn the headings into section headers
decisions.why: 1 heading is plain text where every other page uses a section header, so the page reads as one continuous wall instead of parts.

decisions.label: Tag a document link with the format it opens
decisions.why: 1 link on this page opens a file — 1 PDF — and says nothing about it, while others in the same list carry a tag because their author typed one. The format is read from the file name, so the list stops being half-labelled. No link text changes.

decisions.label: Drop the dash once the link is set apart
decisions.why: 6 of those items separate the link from its description with a dash. The link is now set in the display face at a larger size with a chevron after it, so the dash marks a boundary that is already unmistakable. Only the separator is removed — no word changes.

decisions.label: Separate a link from its description
decisions.why: 14 list items open with a link and then explain it, all at the same weight — so the thing you can click is no easier to find than the sentence about it. The link becomes the item and the explanation sits under it.

decisions.label: Give an unlinked item the same title weight
decisions.why: 1 item sits in a list of links and descriptions without being a link, so it comes out as the only row with no title — which reads as a fault in the list. The title takes the same weight as its neighbours. No link is invented, because there is no address to invent.

decisions.label: Make a loose address look like an address
decisions.why: 1 email address sits in the body of this page rather than in a contact block, drawn exactly like every other link — so the one that opens a mail window looks the same as the ones that go to web pages. The chip carries the same envelope the banner's contact link uses. The address itself does not change.

decisions.label: Use this paragraph as the page description
decisions.why: It is the page’s own opening paragraph, moved into the banner rather than rewritten.

decisions.why: 8 descriptions begin with a small letter, because they used to run on from the link after a dash. The dash is gone and the link now sits above in its own face, so each description opens a line of its own. One character changes and only ever the first.
